body: At three in the morning the night desk of a care home is the only lit place in the building. The woman on it has done the two o’clock round and the next one is not until four. She has boiled the kettle in the little kitchen and not used it. Her brother’s last message is open on her phone and she has read it enough times now that the words have stopped going in at all. She wants to pray about it. She has wanted to pray about it for eleven days. What happens instead, every single time, is that she gets four words in and finds she is simply worrying again, with a religious opening on the front of it.

That state is extremely common and almost nobody describes it out loud, because saying it sounds like a confession of failure. It is not a failure of faith. It is a failure of assembly, and from the inside the two are indistinguishable.

The prayer stations on this band do one thing and do it without interruption: audible prayer, in one language, around the clock. No teaching, no music bed engineered to move anybody, no presenter working the room. Just praying, continuously.

Take continuously literally, because it is the only genuinely interesting thing about the format. There is no programme clock built to hold your attention across a break. There is nothing to catch up on and no episode you have missed. It does not open by greeting you and it will not close by thanking you for listening, because it did not begin when you arrived and it does not stop when you go. What it is, structurally, is an open room with people praying in it, left unlocked. That is a very old idea and it long predates broadcasting: the hours of prayer in monastic houses were an attempt at exactly the same thing with the only technology then available, which was human beings organised in shifts.

The prayer block sits in its own stretch of the dial and every frequency in it is currently in the same condition: HM 355.60 Jubilee Prayers in Swahili, HM 354.20 Jubilee Prayers in Arabic and HM 352.80 Jubilee Prayers in French are assigned and in build, with no audio on any of them yet. Naming them is honest. Sending you there tonight would not be.

It is worth being clear about what a block like that costs and why it is being built anyway. A prayer station has no host to promote, no guest to book, no highlight worth clipping, and nothing whatsoever that will travel well when passed around. By every measure a media operation would normally use it is a bad idea, and it consumes a frequency that could have carried music people would actually share with each other. It is being built because the need it answers keeps no office hours. The band is on every continent, so somewhere it is always three in the morning, and somebody is always awake with something they cannot put down.

Nearly everything else made for religious listeners is now optimised the other way about. It is built to be started, to hold, and to be finished, and the number underneath it is engagement, which is a polite word for whether you stayed. That produces a great deal of good material and it produces one particular blind spot: nothing designed to hold your attention is any use at all to a person who has none left to give it. At three in the morning the last thing somebody in real trouble can manage is to be engaged. They can be present, barely, and that is the whole of what they have.

It is also why each frequency holds one language and does not rotate through several. A person in the state described above is not going to sit through twenty minutes of a language they do not speak in the hope that theirs comes round again before four. They need to be able to arrive already inside it. That is the entire reason for a prayer block arranged by tongue rather than a single station cycling through them, and it is why the numbers are separate and permanent rather than shared.
The obvious modern alternative is an app with guided prayer in it, and some of them are very good indeed. They fail at exactly one moment, and it is this one.

Be fair to them first: they are well made, they are often written by serious people, and between them they have got more prayer into more ordinary days than any quantity of exhortation from a pulpit ever managed. If you can use one, use one. But a guided prayer waits for you to press play, which means it begins because you decided, and at three in the morning deciding is precisely the faculty that has gone. Worse than that, it addresses you. It says now bring to mind, and take a breath, and there you are again, the person who has to produce something. The whole difficulty was that you cannot produce anything. Being asked very gently is still being asked.
You cannot start a thing in the state where starting is what you have lost. You can join a thing already going.

In a two-room house outside Dar es Salaam a mechanic wakes at three because he has woken at three for years and his body no longer asks him about it. His wife is asleep. He goes out and sits on the step. Ordinarily he prays aloud, quietly, in Swahili, because praying inside his own head has never worked for him and never will — he needs to hear it leave. Tonight he cannot start. His eldest has not phoned in a fortnight and he has run out of ways of asking God about it that do not come out sounding like an accusation. So he sits on the step and says nothing, and the nothing goes on for about an hour, and then it begins to get light and he goes in to find his shoes.

He was not refusing to pray. He had lost the first move, which is the move that almost everything else in the Christian life quietly assumes you can still make. Somebody else’s voice, already going, would have handed it back to him.

The honest cost of this format is that it is boring, and there is no version of it that is not boring. It has no arc. It repeats itself. It will pray at length about things that are not your things, in words you would not have chosen, and if it is in a language you do not speak you will not follow a sentence of it. On top of all that, the frequency this article is about has no audio on it whatsoever yet, which is the largest concession in the piece and there is no honest way round it.

The dullness is not a flaw in the format; it is very nearly the format itself. Anything with an arc is asking you to follow it, and following is a kind of work. A station that never develops is a station you can be in the room with while contributing precisely nothing, for as long as you need to contribute nothing, and that is a genuinely rare permission to be given. The liturgical traditions worked this out a long time ago, which is also why people in trouble have always been handed the Psalms to say rather than told to compose something of their own.

So the argument is small and it is practical. Continuous audible prayer exists for the hours in which a person cannot initiate, which are the hours when prayer matters most and is least available to them. It works by lowering the entry from starting to joining. It has to run all the time because the need runs all the time, and it has to sit in one language because the person arriving has nothing left in reserve with which to wait.
None of which is any help at three tomorrow morning unless something is actually on air. So here is what is on air.

The dial carries 121 stations, 46 of them playing tonight, and a fair number of those are formats built for the hours when nobody is at their best — quiet worship, scripture, music left running rather than performed at anybody. The prayer block will join them one language at a time, and the frequencies are already held for it. In the meantime the property that matters at three in the morning is not the genre and never was. It is whether the words are already assembled, and already going, at the moment you get there.

Which points at one frequency in particular: HM 305.40 — Torah Sings, on air now and running live around the clock. It is Torah-rooted worship, which is to say the words are drawn from the text itself rather than from somebody’s reflections on it, and it is sung continuously by a host rather than presented in episodes. That matters at three in the morning for the exact reason this article has been making. You do not have to agree with it, follow its argument, or produce a response to it. The words were assembled a very long time ago by other people, and they are already in the air when you arrive. It is the nearest thing on the dial tonight to an unlocked room with praying going on inside it.

There is nothing to install and no card to go and find. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest, press play, and it plays — it is built deliberately for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have at three in the morning rather than the hardware a demonstration assumes. Add the page to your home screen if you want it a thumb away in the dark, and it opens like anything else on there. And do make an account while you are there. It is free, it keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band finds out which frequencies people are really reaching for — which is how the silent ones get their turn.

So do not save this for a crisis and do not resolve to use it. Put it on tonight, at a volume you can talk over, and let it be running before you need it, because the whole point is that you will not be capable of starting it later. That is the only instruction here. Leave the room unlocked in advance. When three o’clock arrives and the words will not assemble, you will not have to assemble anything — you will only have to be in the room where somebody else already is.
